words.intro: Germans insure more than almost anyone: their teeth, their legal disputes and even their bicycles. Once in your life, you will fill in a claim form, and you will be judged by how well you describe a saucepan.

grammar[0].fact: Germany pays out for a thing called *Hausrat*: everything in your home, down to the spoons. So you may be asked, after a burglary, to list it all. It’s a rare and painful reckoning with your possessions.

grammar[1].fact: Why say *entscheiden* when you can say *eine Entscheidung treffen*? It’s longer, it sounds more important, and it leaves more room for delay. There’s a German word for this too: *Nominalstil*. Your teachers will warn you against it, and then use it.

document.intro: A real enamel plate on the door of an old half-timbered house. It’s a fire insurance plate, and houses used to carry them so the fire brigade knew who’d pay. *Anstalt* is an old word for an institution. The 7 is the house number.
document.fact: Fire insurance is old in Germany: a public fire fund began in Hamburg in 1676. Plates like this one survive on old houses. They were a kind of advertising, and a kind of warning.
reading.title: Schadensmeldung
reading.intro: Max’s washing machine has flooded the flat below. He has to fill in a form for the insurer. Unfortunately, he has asked Lena to help. *Beschreiben Sie den Hergang in vollständigen Sätzen.* This is his third version.
reading.fact: Germans are among the world’s most insured people: a household often has several policies, including *Haftpflicht*, liability, which pays when you break something belonging to someone else. It’s not compulsory, but having none is considered close to reckless. Every German asks: *Bist du haftpflichtversichert?*
